questions.question: What is the difference between `fmt.Printf`, `fmt.Sprintf`, and `fmt.Fprintf`?
questions.title: Choosing a fmt formatting destination
questions.direct_answer: All three apply a format string to arguments, but their destinations differ: `Printf` writes to standard output, `Sprintf` returns the formatted string, and `Fprintf` writes to a supplied `io.Writer`. Use `Sprintf` when text must become a value, `Fprintf` when the caller owns the destination, and avoid hard-coded `Printf` inside reusable library logic unless console output is its actual contract.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether formatting, destination ownership, write errors, and output escaping are distinguished.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Printing directly inside reusable code or assuming formatted text is automatically escaped for its eventual context.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect Fprintf's io.Writer parameter to both testability and destination flexibility.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `Fprintf` writes to an `io.Writer` and returns byte count plus error.
The same verbs and argument rules apply across the three functions.
Choose the destination explicitly at the API boundary.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The `fmt` formatting family separates formatting from destination. `Printf` sends formatted output to standard output and returns the byte count plus any write error. `Sprintf` returns the resulting string, so it has no destination write error. `Fprintf` accepts an `io.Writer`, writes there, and returns count and error.

For example, a command-line `main` function may call `Printf` for user output. A function building an error label can use `Sprintf`. A report renderer should often accept an `io.Writer` and call `Fprintf`, allowing the caller to choose a file, buffer, HTTP response, or test destination. This keeps reusable logic independent of process-global output.

`fmt.Appendf` offers the same formatting style while appending to a byte slice, which can be useful in buffer-oriented code. For one primitive conversion, `strconv` is usually more direct. For fixed strings without formatting, ordinary writes avoid a format string entirely.

Formatting does not make output logging-safe, HTML-safe, SQL-safe, or shell-safe. Escaping and structured logging are separate responsibilities. I choose among these functions by destination and return contract, then choose a domain-specific encoder when output enters a syntax that requires escaping.

sections.title: Formatting is one stage; destination and encoding are others
sections.content:
A format string decides textual representation. Printf fixes the destination to stdout. Sprintf holds the bytes as a returned immutable string. Fprintf delegates destination ownership through `io.Writer`. None of those choices defines escaping for another language.

Separating stages makes functions testable. A writer-based renderer can write into `bytes.Buffer` in a test and a file in production. An HTML template or JSON encoder should own its syntax rather than receiving manually formatted untrusted content.

sections.title: Same formatting, different destination
sections.content:
| Function | Destination | Main result | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fmt.Printf` | Standard output | byte count, error | CLI display |
| `fmt.Sprintf` | Returned string | string | Build a label or message value |
| `fmt.Fprintf` | Supplied `io.Writer` | byte count, error | Reusable renderer |
| `fmt.Appendf` | Supplied byte slice | extended slice | Byte-buffer construction |

questions.question: What do common `fmt` formatting verbs mean in Go?
questions.title: Common fmt verbs and format mistakes
questions.direct_answer: Use `%v` for a default value, `%+v` for field names in structs, `%#v` for Go-syntax-style output, `%T` for the concrete type, `%q` for quoted text, `%s` for strings or byte slices, `%d` for decimal integers, and `%x` for hexadecimal. A mismatched verb produces a `%!` diagnostic in output, and `go vet` catches many constant-format mistakes before runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether formatting intent, diagnostics, conversion, static analysis, and public serialization are separated.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting `%d` to parse numeric text or exposing `%#v` as a stable API response format.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain both runtime `%!` diagnostics and the compile-time assistance provided by go vet.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `%q` quotes strings and runes in an escaped form.
`%s`, `%d`, and `%x` express string, decimal, and hexadecimal intent.
Run `go vet` to catch many format/argument mismatches.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A format verb states how an argument should be represented. `%v` asks for the default form. For structs, `%+v` includes field names, and `%#v` aims at a Go-syntax representation. `%T` reports the concrete type, which is especially useful when an interface holds an unexpected value.

Text often uses `%s`, while `%q` adds Go-style quoting and escapes so empty strings, spaces, and control characters become visible. Decimal integers use `%d`; `%x` and `%X` show hexadecimal. Width and precision refine presentation, such as `%6.2f`, but they do not validate a domain value.

For example, printing a record with `%v`, `%+v`, and `%#v` produces three useful debugging levels, while `%q` distinguishes `" go\n"` from ordinary display. Passing a string to `%d` does not convert it to a number; fmt emits a diagnostic beginning with `%!d`, which can easily leak into logs or responses.

`go vet` analyzes calls whose format strings are known and reports many wrong verbs, missing arguments, and wrapper mistakes. Dynamic format strings still need tests and careful ownership. I use `strconv` for machine numeric conversion, structured log attributes for production logs, and fmt verbs for controlled human-readable formatting.

sections.title: A verb selects representation, not conversion or validation
sections.content:
Fmt receives already typed arguments. It formats them under verb rules and reports mismatches inside the output rather than returning a formatting error for every wrong verb. This design makes development diagnostics visible, while static analysis catches many mistakes earlier.

Representation choice affects privacy and stability. `%+v` or `%#v` can reveal internal fields and should not define a public wire contract. JSON, templates, and structured logging provide stronger schema and escaping guarantees for those boundaries.

sections.title: Useful format views
sections.content:
| Verb | Meaning | Example purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `%v` | Default value | General display |
| `%+v` | Default plus struct field names | Debug a record |
| `%#v` | Go-syntax-style representation | Detailed diagnostics |
| `%T` | Concrete type | Inspect interface content |
| `%q` | Quoted and escaped text/rune | Reveal whitespace |
| `%d` / `%x` | Decimal / hexadecimal integer | Numeric representation |

questions.question: How do `Stringer` and custom formatting work with the `fmt` package?
questions.title: Stringer, error, and custom fmt formatting
questions.direct_answer: For string-compatible verbs, fmt can use an operand's `error` method or `String() string` method; `%#v` can use `GoString() string`, and a type implementing `fmt.Formatter` receives complete control through `Format`. These hooks should be concise, non-panicking, and free of sensitive data. A `String` method on a string-based type must convert to the underlying string before formatting to avoid recursive calls.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether fmt's interface hooks, recursion risk, privacy, and machine-format boundary are understood.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Formatting the receiver as itself inside String, causing unbounded recursion.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe when Formatter is justified beyond the simpler Stringer contract.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The `error` interface supplies `Error() string` for compatible string formatting.
`fmt.Formatter` handles flags, width, precision, and the verb directly.
Convert a string-based receiver before Sprintf to avoid recursion.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The fmt package checks formatting interfaces before falling back to default representation. For string-valid verbs, a value implementing `error` can provide `Error() string`, and a value implementing `fmt.Stringer` can provide `String() string`. `%#v` has a separate `GoStringer` hook. `fmt.Formatter` is the advanced option because its `Format` method receives state, flags, width, precision, and the selected verb.

For example, a `UserID` type can implement `String` to display an identifiable but safe form. Then `%s` or `%v` uses that method. The method should be deterministic and avoid database calls, locks with surprising contention, or secrets, because formatting occurs in logs, errors, and debugging paths where failures are especially harmful.

A classic recursion mistake happens with a defined string type: `func (id UserID) String() string { return fmt.Sprintf("<%s>", id) }`. Formatting `id` as `%s` calls `String` again forever. Converting first—`string(id)`—removes the method set from the formatted operand and produces the intended result.

Custom Formatter is justified when flags or precision have domain meaning; otherwise Stringer is easier to understand. Neither hook should become a wire format accidentally. JSON, database, and protocol encoders need explicit stable contracts even when the same type has a friendly String method.

sections.title: Formatting dispatches through a small behaviour contract
sections.content:
Fmt examines the operand and verb, then gives specialized formatting hooks a chance to produce output. This is ordinary interface-based substitution: a type opts into behaviour by its method set without registering with fmt.

The hook sits on diagnostic paths, so robustness matters. Keep it bounded, avoid recursively formatting the same receiver type, and redact information that should not enter logs. Use explicit encoders for machine contracts rather than relying on a display method.
